subject: Economy
sub_topic: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development — IBRD

concepts.name: IBRD's Founding, Mandate and Historical Context
key_dimensions: Established at Bretton Woods Conference 1944, operational since 1946 — distinction from IMF's operational date
Original mandate: post-WWII reconstruction vs. current mandate shift to development and poverty reduction
IBRD as the oldest institution of the World Bank Group — often confused with 'World Bank' itself
Why IBRD is called a 'development bank' vs. a 'central bank' or 'monetary fund' — conceptual trap

concepts.name: IBRD vs. World Bank vs. World Bank Group — Definitional Clarity
key_dimensions: 'World Bank' in common usage = IBRD + IDA (two institutions only, not all five)
'World Bank Group' = IBRD + IDA + IFC + MIGA + ICSID — UPSC frequently tests this five-institution breakdown
IBRD focuses on middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries; IDA on poorest — eligibility boundary is a classic trap
India's relationship: India borrows from both IBRD and IDA historically; current status as IBRD-only borrower

concepts.name: Membership Structure and Voting Rights in IBRD
key_dimensions: Membership conditionality: a country must first be a member of IMF to join IBRD
Weighted voting system: votes based on capital subscription (shares held) — not one-country-one-vote
USA holds the largest single voting share (~16%), giving it effective veto on major decisions requiring 85% supermajority
India's voting share and rank — relevance to calls for reform of Bretton Woods institutions

concepts.name: IBRD's Capital Structure and Callable Capital Mechanism
key_dimensions: Paid-in capital vs. callable capital distinction — callable capital is a guarantee, not actually paid
IBRD raises most of its funds by issuing bonds in international capital markets, not from member contributions directly
AAA credit rating of IBRD — how callable capital backstop enables this rating
Distinction from IDA which is funded by donor replenishments (grants/concessional contributions)

concepts.name: IBRD Lending Instruments and Loan Types
key_dimensions: Investment Project Financing (IPF) vs. Development Policy Financing (DPF) vs. Program-for-Results (PforR) — three core instruments
IBRD loans are non-concessional (market-based interest rates) unlike IDA credits which are concessional
Loan conditions and structural adjustment requirements — 'conditionality' concept and sovereignty concerns
IBRD does NOT provide grants (only IDA provides grants to eligible countries) — a frequent UPSC trap

concepts.name: IBRD's Role vs. IMF's Role — Functional Differentiation
key_dimensions: IMF = balance of payments support, macroeconomic stability (short-term); IBRD = long-term development finance
IMF lends to all member countries including developed ones; IBRD lends primarily to developing/middle-income nations
Both born at Bretton Woods but with distinct mandates — 'twins with different jobs' analogy
Overlap area: when a country faces debt crisis, both IMF and World Bank may be simultaneously involved — coordination mechanism

concepts.name: Graduation Policy — When Countries 'Graduate' from IBRD
key_dimensions: Graduation = when a country's per capita income exceeds IBRD's operational threshold (currently ~$7,995 GNI per capita)
Graduation is not automatic; depends on access to private capital markets and creditworthiness assessment
Countries can re-access IBRD after crises (e.g., Argentina, Greece considered) — graduation is reversible
India's graduated status from IDA (2014) but continued IBRD borrowing — nuanced status

concepts.name: IBRD and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) — Strategic Alignment
key_dimensions: World Bank Group's twin goals: End extreme poverty by 2030 + Boost shared prosperity — how IBRD operationalizes these
Climate finance commitments: IBRD's role in green bonds and climate-aligned lending
IBRD's Evolution Roadmap (2023) — reforms to increase lending capacity and address global public goods
Criticism: IBRD's conditionalities vs. 'no strings attached' lending by China's development banks — geopolitical dimension

concepts.name: IBRD's Governance Structure — Board and President
key_dimensions: Board of Governors (one per member country, usually finance minister) vs. Board of Executive Directors (25 EDs, day-to-day)
Unwritten convention: World Bank President is always an American; IMF Managing Director is always a European — reform debates
President is nominated by the USA and confirmed by Board — US dominance in selection process
Recent presidents and reform agenda: Jim Yong Kim, David Malpass, Ajay Banga (first non-white president, Indian-American) — current affairs

concepts.name: IBRD and India — Borrowing History and Key Projects
key_dimensions: India is one of the largest borrowers from IBRD historically — infrastructure, health, education projects
India's dual role: borrower from IBRD AND contributor/shareholder
Key sectors: urban infrastructure, renewable energy, social protection, COVID-19 response financing
India's position on IBRD reform — advocating for greater voting share for developing countries

concepts.name: IBRD vs. Regional Development Banks — Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: IBRD (global) vs. ADB, AfDB, IADB, NDB, AIIB (regional) — scope and membership difference
NDB (BRICS bank) and AIIB as 'challengers' to IBRD's dominance — geopolitical context
IBRD has broader sectoral and geographic scope; regional banks have deeper local knowledge
India is a founding member of AIIB and NDB — potential conflict or complementarity with IBRD borrowing

concepts.name: IBRD's Safeguard Policies and Environmental/Social Standards
key_dimensions: Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) 2018 — replaced older Operational Policies
Involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, biodiversity — specific safeguard categories
Criticism of World Bank projects in India (e.g., Narmada Dam controversy, Sardar Sarovar) — historical case study
Inspection Panel mechanism: independent body allowing project-affected communities to file complaints against IBRD

concepts.name: IBRD's Bond Issuance and Role in Global Capital Markets
key_dimensions: IBRD is one of the world's largest issuers of triple-A bonds — intermediary between capital markets and developing countries
Green Bonds: IBRD issued the world's first labeled green bond in 2008 — pioneer status
Sustainable Development Bonds, Social Bonds — IBRD's thematic bond portfolio
How IBRD's AAA rating allows it to on-lend at rates lower than what developing countries could access directly

concepts.name: Conditionality and Policy-Based Lending — Controversies
key_dimensions: Development Policy Loans (DPLs) attached to policy reforms — structural adjustment legacy
Washington Consensus critique: IBRD/IMF prescriptions of privatization, liberalization, deregulation and their mixed outcomes
'Ownership' principle in modern IBRD lending — shift from externally imposed to country-owned reforms
Debt sustainability concerns: has IBRD lending contributed to debt distress in some countries?

concepts.name: IBRD's Relationship with IDA — Synergies and Differences
key_dimensions: IBRD transfers part of its net income to IDA — financial linkage between the two institutions
IDA 20 replenishment (2021) — how IDA funding works differently from IBRD's market borrowing
Blend countries: nations eligible for both IBRD and IDA simultaneously — e.g., Pakistan, Nigeria
IDA graduation to IBRD-only status is a milestone in a country's development — India's 2014 graduation

concepts.name: IBRD and Global Public Goods — Pandemic, Climate, Fragility
key_dimensions: IBRD's expanded role post-COVID: financing vaccines, health systems — departure from traditional infrastructure focus
Crisis Response Window and Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Options (Cat DDO) — disaster preparedness instruments
Fragile and conflict-affected states (FCS): IBRD's limited role (IDA FCS window is primary) — boundary knowledge
Evolution Roadmap 2023: proposal to treat global public goods (pandemics, climate) as core IBRD business

concepts.name: IBRD Capital Adequacy and Calls for Reform
key_dimensions: Periodic General Capital Increases (GCI) — countries negotiate and commit additional capital to IBRD
2018 capital increase ($13 billion) linked to governance reforms including increased voting share for China and other emerging economies
G20 Independent Review of MDBs (2022-23): recommendations to stretch IBRD balance sheet and increase lending headroom
Tension between maintaining AAA rating (requiring capital conservation) and scaling up lending for development needs

concepts.name: IBRD's Knowledge and Technical Assistance Role
key_dimensions: IBRD is not just a lender — it also provides research, data, and policy advice (World Development Report, Doing Business Report)
Doing Business Report discontinued in 2021 due to data manipulation controversy — institutional integrity issue
Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs): strategic documents guiding IBRD's engagement in each country
South-South knowledge exchange programs facilitated by IBRD — non-lending activities

concepts.name: IBRD's Immunities, Privileges and Legal Status
key_dimensions: IBRD has international legal personality — can sue and be sued in member countries' courts
Articles of Agreement grant IBRD immunity from taxation and legal processes in member countries
IBRD is headquartered in Washington D.C. — host country agreement with USA
Dispute resolution: ICSID (another World Bank Group member) handles investor-state disputes, NOT IBRD directly — institutional boundary

concepts.name: IBRD Articles of Agreement — Key Prohibitions and Principles
key_dimensions: Article IV: IBRD can only lend for specific purposes — productive purposes, not military or political
Non-interference principle: IBRD shall not interfere in political affairs of member countries — often tested against conditionality practice
Prohibition on tied loans: IBRD loans should not be conditional on procurement from specific countries
Requirement that loans be guaranteed by member governments or made to governments directly — private sector lending goes through IFC, not IBRD
